messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  (none)

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  (none)

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Carlos, a 58-year-old Latin American forensic analyst, has been struggling with the aftermath of a man-made disaster that occurred nearly six months ago. The event was sudden and violent—a massive explosion at his workplace—that left Carlos with lingering trauma. The night of the disaster is still vivid in Carlos’s mind. He recalls the sound of shattering glass and the deafening boom that seemed to tear through the air, followed by an eerie silence. As he scrambled to safety amidst the chaos, he saw colleagues injured and bleeding, their faces contorted with pain and fear. This event has left him acutely aware of danger in unfamiliar environments. In the weeks following the disaster, Carlos found himself avoiding new or unfamiliar places because he could not assess the level of danger they posed. The uncertainty was paralyzing, and each step outside his comfort zone felt like a potential trap waiting to spring. He had come to believe that if he were to encounter another situation like the one at work, he would be unable to react appropriately, making him feel jumpy and easily startled. His body remains in constant tension, as though it is always on alert for the next threat. Even simple tasks now seem daunting. The slightest noise—a door slamming or a car backfiring—can send his heart racing and his palms sweating. He finds himself hypervigilant, constantly scanning his surroundings for signs of impending danger. This heightened state of alertness has also led to feelings of incompetence and self-doubt. Carlos was once known for his sharp analytical skills and his ability to remain calm under pressure. Now, he feels that his reactions since the event show that he is a lousy coper. He fears that this incident has revealed his true inadequacies and that he can no longer perform at the level he once did. This belief has begun to erode his confidence in himself as a forensic analyst. In addition, Carlos’s worldview has shifted dramatically. The explosion made him realize how fragile life can be and how easily it can be shattered by human recklessness. He now sees the world as inherently dangerous, a place where threats lurk around every corner. This perception of danger is compounded by his belief that he cannot adequately protect himself or those close to him. The impact on his work has been significant. Carlos’s avoidance of unfamiliar places means that he often declines field assignments and prefers to stay in familiar environments. His wife, who had always admired his resilience and strength, notices the change in him but doesn’t quite understand why he is so different now. Their conversations have become strained as she struggles to bridge the gap between their present realities. What finally brought Carlos to seek help was a recent incident where he nearly missed an important meeting because he hesitated to leave his house for fear of encountering another threat. This realization that his condition was affecting not just his work but also his personal life pushed him to acknowledge that he needed support. Carlos is most afraid that the disaster will define him and rob him of who he once was—a competent, confident professional and a loving husband. He hopes for a return to some semblance of normalcy where he can feel safe again without having to constantly question his ability to cope with life’s uncertainties.
